sections.html:
Great Falls is the county seat of Cascade County and the only city in it. Belt, Cascade and Neihart are the small towns, and 84,414 people lived here at the 2020 census. Beyond town limits you find places like Black Eagle, Sand Coulee, Simms, Ulm and Vaughn. A city lot and a rural house are very different listings. Whoever buys the rural one will want to hear about the well, the septic system and how the road is plowed in January.

Malmstrom Air Force Base shapes local demand more than any other employer. It has 3,896 assigned personnel (3,371 military and 525 civilian) and 1,116 privatized housing units. Many buyers and sellers here move when base assignments change, so a sale on a tight clock is common.

sections.h2: Selling on a short move timeline
sections.html:
Got orders? Give every buyer your report date at the first conversation. A mortgage buyer needs an appraisal and underwriting before closing day. A cash buyer needs neither, so the closing can land on whatever date works for your move, and the house is accepted in its current condition, which saves you from fixing things in the final weeks.

Property tax gets settled at closing no matter who buys. Pull these together before you list or accept an offer:

  • Your latest tax statement and any protest or AB-26 paperwork.
  • Proof of homestead enrollment, if you have it.
  • The orders that set your move date, if a transfer drives the sale.

sections.h2: 2026 tax rates on Cascade County homes
sections.html:
For 2026, Montana sorts homes into classes with different rates. A slice of value is taxed at the rate for its bracket. The county then multiplies the result by the combined mills of every district covering your address, which is why two houses with the same value can get different bills. Your tax statement shows what you actually pay.

Property type (2026)Tax rate on market value
Primary residence or long-term rental, first $378,0000.76 percent
Same, $378,001 to $756,0000.90 percent
Same, $756,001 to $1,511,9991.10 percent
Same, above $1,511,9991.90 percent
Second home, short-term rental, vacant residential lot1.90 percent
Long-term rental multifamily dwelling1.10 percent

The lower bracketed rate is the homestead rate. It covers single-family houses, townhomes, condos and manufactured homes on up to one acre, provided the owner occupies the home for seven months or more each year.

Your homestead status is not a permanent feature of the house. After a sale, the approved rate rides along until December 31 of that year. The next owner then has to file an application of their own, and for tax year 2027 the enrollment window ends March 1, 2027.

Landlords who buy have their own path. A rental earns the bracketed rate if tenants stay 28 days or more and the house is rented at least seven months of the year, but the owner must still apply in the window. Skip the form, or switch to short stays, and the 1.90 percent flat rate applies.

  • Seller: hand the title company your last tax bill and homestead approval.
  • Owner-occupant buyer: file the homestead application before March 1.
  • Long-term landlord buyer: apply during the rental window and plan on seven months of qualifying tenancy.

The bill comes in two halves. The first is payable until 5 p.m. on November 30 (or thirty days past the postmark on your notice, whichever is later), and the second until 5 p.m. on May 31. Those dates come from Montana Code 15-16-102. A deadline that falls on a Saturday or holiday slides to 5 p.m. the next business day.

If the house is your primary residence, you can spread the year over seven equal installments instead. Payments fall at the end of each month: November 30, December 31, January 31, February 28, March 31, April 30 and May 31. Cascade County's treasurer lists two payment plans, and this is the one for real estate. Call the treasurer's office to sign up.

Miss a deadline and the unpaid amount picks up a 2 percent penalty and interest of 5/6 of 1 percent every month. Back taxes do not block you from paying the current year, though a payment aimed at delinquency is credited to the oldest year first. Clearing this year's bill leaves the lien on an earlier year in place.

The treasurer sends the bill, but the state sets the value, so a disagreement about value goes to the Department of Revenue. You have 30 days from the date printed on your classification and appraisal notice to pick one of two paths: send Form AB-26 for an informal review, or skip ahead and file with the county clerk and recorder for a hearing at the county tax appeal board.

Values for the 2025 to 2026 cycle are pinned to January 1, 2024. Build your case around that date. Useful proof includes your own estimate of what the house was worth then, a purchase price from within six months of it, a fee appraisal, comparable sales and listings, and a builder's cost breakdown if you remodeled. Start by checking square footage and room counts on Property.MT.gov, then phone your Department of Revenue field office to talk it through with an appraiser.

An unhappy result from the informal review can go to the county tax appeal board, which county commissioners appoint and which operates independently. After that come the Montana Tax Appeal Board and then district court. One trap: to keep any refund alive, you must file a written protest with the treasurer and pay the disputed amount on time. Cascade County's protest form is due before the first Monday in June, or within 30 days of a classification notice or review decision.

Back taxes on real estate turn into a lien that the treasurer enforces. On a mobile home, the treasurer can instead go for a writ of execution, although the owner is normally offered a chance to pay everything or enter a payment program first.

With a house, the easy route is to sell and let the sale pay it off. The title company looks up the tax record and deducts any overdue tax, penalty and interest when funds are distributed. A cash buyer makes this smoother because no lender is waiting to approve the payoff.

In practice: ask the treasurer's office what you owe today, hand that figure to the title company, then read the closing statement and confirm the tax line matches before you sign.

faqs.q: Who handles property tax bills in Cascade County?
faqs.a: The county treasurer's office collects and bills the tax. The Montana Department of Revenue sets valuation and handles assessment appeals, so questions about appraised value go to the department.

faqs.q: Can I pay Cascade County property tax in seven payments?
faqs.a: Yes, if you enroll in the alternative schedule for a primary residence. One-seventh is due on the last day of each month from November 30 through May 31, under Montana Code 15-16-122. The county application form must be filed to enroll.

faqs.q: What is the penalty for late property tax in Montana?
faqs.a: Delinquent tax draws interest at 5/6 of 1 percent per month and a 2 percent penalty. Taxes are delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 30 for the first half and after 5 p.m. on May 31 for the second half.

faqs.q: Does a buyer keep my homestead tax rate?
faqs.a: Not automatically. The rate stays on the property through the end of the calendar year of the sale, and the new owner must submit a homestead application to keep it for the next year.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Cascade County house for cash if taxes are owed?
faqs.a: Yes. Unpaid taxes, penalty and interest come out of the proceeds at closing, and the title company confirms the amount with the county treasurer.
